EXCLUSIVE: Disney Live Action has added two to the cast of Lilo & Stitch 2 : young up-and-comer Teagan Meredith ( Fallout ) and the Spider-Man franchise's Jacob Batalon .

The studio also confirmed returning cast, including Maia Kealoha as Lilo, along with Courtney B. Vance, Kaipo Dudoit, Amy Hill, Tia Carrere and Billy Magnussen.

Character details for the new additions are being kept under wraps. There's no word yet on the plot of the sequel. articles.content:
"Spider-Man: Brand New Day" broke box office records when it hit theaters over the summer, but several scenes were left on the cutting room floor. One of those included Rosario Dawson 's character Claire Temple, aka the Night Nurse, from Netflix's Marvel shows. Now, "Brand New Day" is getting a theatrical re-release that will re-add some of those deleted scenes, and Dawson confirmed that she will be in the extended cut.

"It’s a brand new BRAND NEW DAY with our friendly neighborhood Spider-Man!" Dawson wrote on Instagram with a photo of her character and Tom Holland's wall-crawler. "So excited to enjoy this record-breaking movie on the big screen (starting on December 4th) with an extended cut of new scenes and surprises… Ahhhh! Join me in getting tickets NOW!!! #SpiderManBrandNewDay PS: mom can finally share her BTS photos." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories China Box Office: 'Resident Evil' Holds Top Spot for Fourth Straight Frame as 2014's 'John Wick' Debuts in Third

It appears that Spidey will visit the Night Nurse at some point in "Brand New Day," perhaps to get his haywire spider powers checked up on. Or, he might get some medical attention after he faces off against Scorpion (Michael Mando), Jean Grey (Sadie Sink), Hulk (Mark Ruffalo), Punisher (Jon Bernthal) or one of the several other super-powered fighters in the movie.

Dawson debuted the character, a nurse who specializes in aiding heroes, in Season 1 of Netflix's "Daredevil" series, starring Charlie Cox. She was a series regular, then returned for an episode of "Jessica Jones" before joining the main casts of "Luke Cage," "Iron Fist" and "The Defenders." In fact, just getting through the show can be such a hectic ordeal for the host that they’re assigned someone to manage their schedule, keep them fed and make sure they’re in the right place and wearing the right costume at the right time. It turns out it’s the same employee every week. Her name is Donna Richards, and she’s apparently seen all the famous people naked.

During a recent episode of Good Hang with Amy Poehler , Richards and her role on the show came up after guest Jack Black talked about her hunting down an Italian chopped salad for him because he was starving between dress rehearsal and the live show. Apparently she’s there to make sure the host is relaxed, comfortable and dressed to perform. Sometimes that means making sure they’ve eaten, and sometimes that means physically yanking clothes on and off them during frantic costume changes between sketches . Here’s a portion of what Poehler said…

She has this really specific job that’s like part nurse, part coach where she kinda grabs you and dresses you from scene to scene. She has your whole show in her hand. She makes sure you can do it. She is the one that if you pass out or you forgot something and turn to her and say I don’t remember, she would have you. She’s your wrangler. She’s seen everybody naked. She’s seen every star naked.

SNL fans are very familiar with the work it takes to pitch, write and rehearse the show every week , but there’s a lot less familiarity around the actual mechanics of making the live show happen. It’s ultimately because of people like Richards and other unsung heroes who make sure their more famous co-workers are physically able to go out there and make us laugh. It’s better for everyone if Jack Black is worried about being funny and not worried about remembering which outfit he’s supposed to get into next and which wig it pairs with.

During the same conversation, Poehler said Richards could write a great book just recounting all of the ridiculous requests that she’s gotten since she started on the show. Apparently, Black asking for an Italian chopped salad without onions is incredibly tame compared to the nonsense she’s normally asked to do, but fortunately, she’s been able to weather those storms and build amazing relationships with cast members and many of the celebrities who have hosted.

Tina Fey made sure she got her moment to appear on camera during SNL ’s 50th Anniversary , and she’s been the subject of a bunch of fun interviews like this where cast members and celebrities shout her out. She’s even apparently developed a fun little bond with Jason Momoa who has come and visited her on a few different occasions.

I can’t wait to see what the talented actress is able to see, thanks in part to Richards who will apparently clothe her, feed her and let her exclusively focus on crushing her lines.

Grammy winner Edgar Barrera has signed with Fortress Talent Management for film and television representation.

Barrera's signing comes after he recently made history as the most-awarded individual at the Latin Grammys , with a record 33 wins.

The songwriter and producer has helped craft global hits, collaborating with some of the industry's biggest artists, including Bad Bunny, Karol G, Shakira, Peso Pluma, Grupo Frontera, and Maluma, among others.

The sequel comes from an original script by Quentin Tarantino , and stars Brad Pitt under the direction of Se7en and Fight Club ’s David Fincher . Talk about a dream trio! The reviews just dropped for the 1977-set flick, and a lot of people are bringing up something that could have been that I thought about myself.

One massive pro of it being a movie is that film buffs can experience the crime-comedy on IMAX screens next week, ahead of it being available to stream with a Netflix subscription in December. However, it definitely feels like there’s a bigger world Tarantino has created that the film didn't have time to fully get to. Cliff Booth has an incredible cast that features some especially memorable parts for Elizabeth Debicki, as a talent agent and the object of Cliff’s affections, and Scott Caan, who plays a popular TV star who needs Cliff’s particular set of skills. articles.title: What's Taking the BioShock Movie So Long? Director Reveals It's the Same Problem Other Video Games Have
articles.summary: BioShock's shift from video game to big-screen movie is something that's been talked about for years now, and it clearly hasn't been easy. Attempts have been made since the game first released back in 2008 to bring it to life, with filmmakers like Gore Verbinski attached at one point and even Oscar-winner Guillermo del Toro […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google BioShock 's shift from video game to big-screen movie is something that's been talked about for years now , and it clearly hasn't been easy. Attempts have been made since the game first released back in 2008 to bring it to life, with filmmakers like Gore Verbinski attached at one point and even Oscar-winner Guillermo del Toro giving it the old college try . Despite almost two decades of trying, though, nothing has been made. Netflix has been attempting to get their own version of the ground for a few years with The Hunger Games franchise director Francis Lawrence attached, and the filmmaker has finally admitted they have a problem.

Speaking with Empire , Lawrence reiterated that the BioShock film is still being worked out and they're "trying to crack it" but this is hardly an update on the film's status at all . That said, Lawrence did reveal what the hold-up is in figuring out how to make it work, confirming that like almost every other video game movie, creating a main character for the story is proving to be its biggest challenge. “That's been the trick: creating the character almost out of whole cloth,” Lawrence added. “Who this person is – what is their emotional journey?”

As fans who played the game will recall, the original BioShock put players in the shoes of Jack, a faceless protagonist that was something of a cypher for the larger machinations of Andrew Ryan and his underwater city of Rapture . Eventually his backstory is revealed, confirming his actual connections to what's going on in the plot, but for the most part the game relies on player choice to determine its ending and allows you to fill in the gaps of what kind of person Jack really is.

That in mind, it's easy to see why turning Jack into a relatable protagonist with his own storyline (before all the twists and turns) is something that would be tough to figure out for the movie. On top of it all, making the protagonist himself relatable and worth spending two hours with has to come on top of recreating a distinct world with unique lore, wild monsters, and even the superpowers that he unlocks for himself along the way.

“I think one of the biggest challenges is that we really want to honour the spirit of the game, its themes, the mythology of the world, and the people who inhabit it," Lawrence added, indicating that the conversations every BioShock fan has had about bringing the game to life is one they've already engaged with.

As gamers know well, though, creating a wholly relatable movie character out of a video game protagonist has been a problem for adaptations for the past thirty years. It's one reason why the stigma of video game movies managed to stick around as long as it did, on top of having to create a whole narrative on top of something that didn't actually have one. That said, BioShock has done a lot of the heavy lifting for the movie in terms of the larger plot and the look of the world, and it would have been easy to fart out a movie that just replicated its visual aesthetic and had no real character at the center. Knowing they don't want to make something that easy is a good sign.

For those wondering why Rockstar Games hasn't licensed Grand Theft Auto for a movie or TV show, this is probably why.

Grand Theft Auto VI has already generated an incredible $1.84 billion in sales, according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower .

That's more than Christopher Nolan 's blockbuster The Odyssey made during its entire global run ($1.80 billion).

The GTA 6 's eye-popping sales figure may already be outdated. While Sensor Tower updated its tracker Thursday, the underlying charts appear to show sales only through Tuesday, Nov. 17 — meaning the $1.84 billion estimate seemingly doesn't account for the final day before launch (when all those glowing reviews were published) or today (when the game was actually released). blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Business 'Grand Theft Auto VI' Has a Small 'Deadpool' Connection Business 'GTA VI' Industry Domination Will Not End Anytime Soon

Therefore, the current GTA 6 sales number is very likely over $2 billion. In case you're curious, the GTA 6 revenue split is 75 percent from PS5 sales and 25 percent for Xbox.

And GTA games tend to have very, very long tails. GTA 5 was released 13 years ago and has generated an estimated $5.4 billion in lifetime revenue (plus an additional $5.4 billion in revenue during that period from GTA Online), according to The Wall Street Journal . Even over the last four years, GTA 5 has averaged $400 million in sales … for, again, a game released in 2013. articles.title: Sequels, Subtitles and Spring Releases: How the Best Picture Race Is Rewriting the Academy’s Playbook
articles.summary: Somebody at every awards season party, and everybody on the internet, will tell you why a movie can’t grab a best picture nomination — or even win the prize. It opened too early. It’s a sequel. It has subtitles. It made no money. It’s a documentary. And then the Academy goes and proves everyone wrong. […]
articles.content:
Somebody at every awards season party, and everybody on the internet, will tell you why a movie can’t grab a best picture nomination — or even win the prize. It opened too early. It’s a sequel. It has subtitles. It made no money. It’s a documentary.

And then the Academy goes and proves everyone wrong.

With the fall festivals in the rearview mirror and the holiday corridor still loading, it’s time to take a look at the best picture race. Christopher Nolan’s “ The Odyssey ” holds the top spot on Variety’s best picture chart and nearly every pundit’s list. But the margin between No. 1 and No. 20 feels thinner than it has in years. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories China Box Office: 'Resident Evil' Holds Top Spot for Fourth Straight Frame as 2014's 'John Wick' Debuts in Third

A24 has many films in the projected lineup. Warner Bros., the reigning champion after its “One Battle After Another” win, with a new boss at the helm of the company, Skydance CEO David Ellison, is keeping Denis Villeneuve’s franchise finale, “ Dune: Part Three ,” close to the vest until December.

And we’re still waiting for Robert Eggers’ “Werwulf,” with Aaron Taylor-Johnson. That film could shake up the race once voters finally get a look at it, and, for argument’s sake, so can “Avengers: Doomsday” from the Russo brothers.

That leaves 20 to 30 films chasing 10 slots, each making its strongest case for why it belongs. Standing in the way are the old rules, and this season is poised to test every one of them.

SUMMER BLOCKBUSTERS FADE BY THE WINTER

Nolan has already broken this rule himself. Universal Pictures’ “Oppenheimer” opened in July 2023 and won seven Oscars the following March. Three years later, “The Odyssey,” the adaptation of Homer’s Greek epic, has the footprint that can lead the nominations field, with an eye on the record 16 nominations “Sinners” set last season. As Odysseus, Matt Damon anchors the voyage home; co-stars Anne Hathaway and Samantha Morton are both tracking for supporting actress recognition, while John Leguizamo and Robert Pattinson are legitimate supporting actor threats. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The bigger question is whether five months of fresher challengers will wear it down.

SEQUELS HAVE DIFFICULTY WINNING

That’s because only two have. “The Godfather Part II” (1974) followed the 1973 best picture winner, “The Godfather,” and “The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King” (2003) remains the only sequel to win after its earlier chapters fell short. The latter provides the playbook for Warner Bros.’ “Dune: Part Three,” which arrives after Villeneuve was left out of the directing lineup for both previous installments. Almost nobody has seen the finale, but Zendaya’s expanded role gives it an acting hook the earlier chapters lacked.

Further down the list, Netflix’s “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” tests the same rule, with David Fincher directing a Quentin Tarantino script based on his 2019 hit “Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood.”

SUBTITLES AND STREAMERS MUST CLEAR HURDLES

Bong Joon Ho’s “Parasite” remains the only non-English-language film to win best picture. Netflix is still waiting for its first, after coming painfully close with “Roma” (2018) and “Emilia Pérez” (2024). Enter the Cannes sensation “La Bola Negra,” the streamer’s Spanish-language drama from Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi. It has Penélope Cruz in the supporting actress conversation, singer-turned-actor Guitarricadelafuente emerging as one of the season’s breakout performers and an international feature campaign supported by a passionate base. It has the texture of a film that could finally get Netflix a win.

Neon won with “Parasite” and “Anora,” both Palme d’Or winners, and it has this year’s Palme winner, too: Cristian Mungiu’s drama “Fjord,” starring Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve. But its slot is not a sure thing in the best picture race with any number of international contenders waiting for a late surge, including Lee Chang-dong’s “Possible Love” from South Korea, Andrey Zvyagintsev’s “Minotaur” from Mubi and Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s “All of a Sudden,” also from Neon.

COMEDIES DON’T GET TAKEN SERIOUSLY blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Then again, not all of these comedies are funny. Martin McDonagh is back for another round with “Wild Horse Nine,” following “The Banshees of Inisherin” (2022), which went home empty-handed despite nine nominations. John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell deliver the kind of performances that could get the actors’ branch buzzing.

A24 is doubling down on laughs. “The Invite” has director and star Olivia Wilde vying for at least two nominations, along with her ensemble. Jesse Eisenberg’s “The Debut” features best actress front-runner Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti, who is tracking for his third Oscar nom and possible first win. The indie label also has “Club Kid,” from debut director Jordan Firstman, looking for awards season love after declaring itself a drama for the Golden Globes.

Meanwhile, Mike Leigh’s “Tender Loving Care,” from Bleecker Street, is entering the Golden Globes race as a comedy, but is more likely to leave audiences in tears than have them laughing.

DOCUMENTARIES AND CARTOONS ARE SPILLING OUT OF THEIR OWN CATEGORIES

No documentary has ever been nominated for best picture, and three animated films have, with none winning. A24’s “You Can See Everything,” from Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, looks more like a sure thing by the day after winning over audiences at industry screenings. It doesn’t hurt that it has become one of the biggest-grossing documentaries in decades.

Laika’s stop-motion epic “Wildwood” is the rare animated feature with a credible best picture argument. Voters have shown they’ll go there when the craft is undeniable.

SPRING RELEASES CAN BE FORGOTTEN

“Everything Everywhere All at Once” opened in March and swept the Oscars the following year. Amazon MGM’s “Project Hail Mary” opened in March, too, and Phil Lord and Christopher Miller’s adaptation of Andy Weir’s novel is the crowd-pleaser of this race. Crowd-pleasers can survive the preferential ballot, especially with Ryan Gosling firmly in the best actor conversation. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Antoine Fuqua’s “Michael,” from Lionsgate, opened in April and became the highest-grossing biopic of all time. Jaafar Jackson hopes to crack the best actor race for playing his uncle, Michael Jackson, while Colman Domingo’s turn as patriarch Joe Jackson is in the supporting actor conversation.

ONE PERFORMANCE CAN CARRY A PICTURE

Don’t tell the actors’ branch. It’s the Academy’s largest, and it has a way of carrying its favorites across the categories. Neon’s “Artificial” has the supporting actor front-runner in Andrew Garfield’s portrayal of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Focus Features acquired “Elsinore” over the summer and hopes Andrew Scott’s towering performance as Ian Charleson can carry it into the best picture race.

Pedro Pascal in Tony Gilroy’s “Behemoth!” and Inde Navarrette in the horror breakout “Obsession” are among the likeliest performers to pull their films into other categories. The same goes for newcomer Anthony Ippolito, so authentic as Sylvester Stallone in Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky” — it’s the kind of underdog story voters love. John Turturro’s performance in “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” from Sony Pictures Classics is also in the best actor conversation.

A few others are flying under the radar but still looking for a defining moment this season. Sumerian Pictures’ “Josephine” won the Grand Jury Prize at Sundance, while Apple’s “Being Heumann” finished as the second runner-up for the People’s Choice Award at TIFF.

The lesson of the past few seasons is that the race is never settled in November. It just looks that way.

articles.title: Marvel's Incredible Hulk Got the Worst Kind of TV Ending, But Returned Like No One Expected
articles.summary: TV tends to be less than generous when it comes to wrapping up superhero stories. Sometimes the show we love gets a proper send-off, a satisfying ending, and the hero gets to do one last rescue. Other times, the network simply pulls the plug and leaves everybody wondering what happened next. Bill Bixby's The Incredible […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google TV tends to be less than generous when it comes to wrapping up superhero stories. Sometimes the show we love gets a proper send-off, a satisfying ending, and the hero gets to do one last rescue. Other times, the network simply pulls the plug and leaves everybody wondering what happened next. Bill Bixby's The Incredible Hulk got the second treatment, which is especially unfortunate when you consider how much viewers had invested in David Banner's seemingly endless search for a cure.

In a twist of irony, the Hulk story did not end on television. After CBS pulled the plug on the weekly series, Banner and his oversized green other half re-emerged, not in a series wrap-up, but in a string of made-for-television movies that took the story in astonishingly different directions. He even managed to bring us a few familiar comic book heroes while he was at it. While some may have considered the closure of the original series odd, the way in which this television comeback was played out is perhaps even more astonishing. And if you're a Hulk fan, you'll want to check out the equally great Hulk cartoon series that was surprisingly accurate to the Marvel Comics series.

The Incredible Hulk debuted in 1977 with a bit of a twist on the typical superhero fare viewers might have been anticipating. Bill Bixby portrayed David Banner as a conflicted scientist on the run, a character who drove from town to town in desperate search of a cure. When he lost control to rage or stress, it was Lou Ferrigno who appeared as the big green Hulk. When reporter Jack McGee, played by Jack Colvin, kept hounding the elusive beast across the country, Banner had yet another reason to keep running. The series ran for five seasons on CBS and developed a loyal following. Yet its eventual departure didn't give viewers the kind of finale that usually comes with a long-running television adventure. CBS decided the series had run its course, and the cancellation left Banner's story hanging.

For me, the show's introduction was absolutely incredible. If you've never seen it, do yourself a favor and check it out. The lack of CGI also added an incredible sense of realism, and it genuinely frightened me when I first watched it as a wee little lad. Even today, I can appreciate the practical production techniques the show used, and it remains one of my favorite Marvel TV shows—even more so than many of Disney's current iterations.

The last episode, "A Minor Problem," has an almost overly subtle title, considering that it is the final episode of the regular series. Banner arrives in a town dealing with an E. coli outbreak and does his best to support the victims. By the end of the episode he is back on the road and back in search of a cure; the episode features neither the big showdown with McGee, any further advancement of Banner's research, nor any resolution for the character. It wasn’t meant as a series finale, but it would be the last episode CBS would air. Johnson, the series creator, had a concept for a finale that would have given Banner a way out of the transformations, but CBS declined it. When your premise involves a man's search for a cure, a series finale with Banner going nowhere quickly becomes a rather unsatisfactory end.

However, the story of Banner was not finished with those events; television would assist in the next chapter. In 1988, Bill Bixby and Lou Ferrigno returned for The Incredible Hulk Returns , a made-for-TV movie that brought the characters back to NBC. This time, Banner wasn't just dealing with his familiar green problem. He also encountered Donald Blake and his rather unusual connection to Thor. Played by Eric Allan Kramer, the Norse god brought a whole new superhero into the world of Bixby's television series. It was a pretty remarkable development for viewers who had spent years watching Banner travel from town to town. Suddenly, the show had another Marvel hero running around, complete with a magical hammer and an entirely different mythology. The movie even served as a potential launching point for a Thor television series, although that never happened. Apparently, one superhero wasn't quite enough for Banner's comeback.

Marvel wasn't finished experimenting with the format, either. The following year brought The Trial of the Incredible Hulk , which introduced Rex Smith as Matt Murdock and his masked identity as Daredevil. John Rhys-Davies also appeared as Wilson Fisk, better known as the Kingpin. That's quite a collection of Marvel characters for a television movie that began with David Banner trying to get his life back together. Bixby directed the film himself and continued to expand the world of the original series. Then came The Death of the Incredible Hulk in 1990, which finally gave Banner's long journey a definitive ending. articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Netflix is continuing to mine content from some of the most acclaimed cult-hit properties of the 1980s, 1990s and 2000s. After turning The Witcher and The Sandman into acclaimed hits, Netflix is taking on Grendel , the comic book series that author Matt Wagner first launched in 1982. Grendel has been an unusual icon in comics: the publishing rights have taken several sharp turns, while the sporadic nature of the character's books and lore is a puzzle not every fan has put together. So what is Netflix doing now that so many other failed adaptations couldn't?

Grendel will be adapted as an animated series by studio Bobbypills, which produces DC's Creature Commandos , with Bobak Esfarjani ( Alien: Earth, Widow's Bay ) acting as showrunner, writer, and executive producer. Now Netflix is releasing full details on the series and who is invovled, which you can read below.

“ Grendel has been at the forefront of independent comics for over forty years, and we’re thrilled to bring Matt Wagner’s creation to Netflix,” John Derderian, Vice President, Animation Series + Kids & Family TV at Netflix, said in a statement. “Like the comic, this animated series will break the traditional superhero mold just as Matt's time-honored comic book has always done. Bobak, Dark Horse Entertainment and Bobbypills are bold storytellers who love this world as much as its fans do, and we’re so excited to partner with them to bring this story to screen.”

Dark Horse Comics was the publisher that picked up Grendel and relaunched it in 1992 after the comic's original publisher, Comico, went bankrupt at the end of the '80s. Chris Tongue, Tim Wiesch, and Jay Komas of Dark Horse Entertainment will be attached as executive producers, alongside Matt Wagner and Lydia Antonini.

"It’s incredibly exciting to see my creation finally make this leap to the animated screen!" Matt Wagner wrote in his statment. "Netflix’s dynamic new series retains the source material’s dark adult themes and also brings a fresh and thrilling approach to the narrative. This is Grendel as I’ve always wanted to see the character portrayed—a hyper-kinetic level of action, bracing explosions of violence and a poignant engaging storyline.”

Grendel has followed several characters who have taken up the titular mantle and been tragically influenced by it. It started with Hunter Rose, an author who moonlights as a masked assassin and eventually becomes the head of New York City's organized crime world.

The Netflix series follows the framework of the original character and story. As per the show's logline: "After the woman he loves is shockingly murdered, Hunter Rose devotes himself to one thing: vengeance. But as he tears through street gangs, the elite, and New York City’s supernatural underworld in pursuit of her killer, a chance at a real life forces him to choose: walk away from ultimate power, or become the very monster he hunts."

Grendel is in development at Netflix. No release date has been set yet.

articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Vice City is undoubtedly the most prominent region in Grand Theft Auto 6's expansive world of Leonida. However, for those who have been booting up GTA 6 for themselves today, it might come as a surprise that the game doesn't open in Vice City. Instead, many of the earliest hours of GTA 6 revolve around Jason, as he works as a drug runner within the Leonida Keys.

Naturally, for those who are primarily following the main missions of Grand Theft Auto 6 , it might be easy to wonder when Jason and Lucia actually end up finding their way into Vice City. To that end, there are multiple answers to this question, each of which simply depends on your own playstyle.

If you're looking to check out Vice City in GTA 6 as early as possible, you're free to drive there in Chapter 1 as soon as the game's world becomes available to you. Upon opening your map, you'll see where Vice City is broadly located and you'll be able to drop a marker on it that will direct your path. While it's quite out of the way when compared to the Leonida Keys and its surroundings, GTA 6 doesn't prevent you from making a trip into the city right away if you so choose.

That being said, much of what Vice City offers to you won't immediately be on display to you if you visit it in this manner. Any connections that you might establish later in GTA 6 aren't opened up to you at this point, and many of the clothing stores and other shops that Vice City offers tend to be far more expensive than others you'll see around Leonida. Because of how small your pool of money is as you start GTA 6 , this will make your options quite limited if you instantly go to Vice City.

As expected, as you progress through GTA 6's story, Vice City becomes a much more prominent place for you to run around, with the majority of its narrative taking place within the downtown area. Outside of a brief mission in Chapter 1 that sees Jason and Lucia partying with friends in Vice City, you won't truly head into town until the tail end of Chapter 2 and the start of Chapter 3. Once you reach this point, you'll then unlock a safehouse in the city, along with a number of other side activities and points of interest.

Personally, I didn't visit Vice City for myself when playing Grand Theft Auto 6 until the story took me there. I ended up appreciating this moment in the game quite a bit more because of it, as the process of first driving up to Vice City is quite cinematic. In addition, Jason and Lucia have to tuck away a good amount of money before they are able to head to Vice City for themselves, which makes the process of finally getting into the city feel like a greater achievement in their journey. While I imagine many playing GTA 6 will want to visit the iconic locale sooner rather than later, for those who hold off on doing so, I think it could feel all the more rewarding once you do get into Vice City's limits.

articles.title: NBC Shakes Up Thanksgiving Broadcast With 9 Broadway Shows Performing a Medley
articles.summary: 'Wicked,' 'Chicago,' 'Hamilton,' 'Schmigadoon!' and 'The Lost Boys' are among the shows participating.
articles.content:
NBC is making a big change for Broadway performers in this year’s Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.

Rather than featuring individual performances, the telecast has gathered nine Broadway shows to sing a 10-minute medley at the top of the show created exclusively for this year’s parade. The shows participating in the medley include several long-runners, in the case of Wicked , Chicago , Hamilton , The Book of Mormon and Aladdin, as well as Schmigadoon! and The Lost Boys , new musicals that both opened last season. The current revival of The Rocky Horror Show will perform, as well as former cast members from Rent, which recently held a 30th anniversary reunion concert.

The medley, which will be introduced by Julianne Hough (who is starring in the upcoming Broadway revival of Damn Yankees) , is described as taking “viewers on a musical journey through Broadway past and present, filled with beloved songs and Easter eggs for theater fans to discover along the way.”

Tom Kitt, the Tony Award-winning composer of Next to Normal , and creative producer Sarah O’Gleby, choreographer on Shucked , arranged the medley. The performances air on Peacock and NBC at 8:30 a.m. in all time zones.

The change opens up performing on the telecast to more shows than usual, with last year’s parade only featuring three Broadway shows, even as it remains unclear how much time each show will get in the spotlight and if they'll perform numbers from their own show. It also shines a light on the long-runners, which is atypical as the performance is typically used to highlight shows that opened within the prior season.

Performing on the telecast is coveted, as it gives Broadway shows rare exposure on national television, with more than 34 million viewers tuning into last year’s parade on NBC. It's seen as a major means to boost ticket sales as the shows enter into their lucrative holiday weeks, and now opens up that option for some long-runners that have fallen from former box office highs, such as Wicked and Aladdin .

In addition to Broadway performers, the parade will feature performances from Megan Moroney, Teddy Swims and the Radio City Rockettes. Paddington The Musical , set to open on Broadway in the spring, is also scheduled for a special appearance.

Natasha Bedingfield, Baha Men, Blues Traveler, DEVO, Jimmy Fallon & The Roots, Feid, EJAE, Mckenna Grace, Indigo Girls, Icona Pop, JoJo, Wyclef Jean, Queen Latifah, Il Volo, Natalie Merchant, Jamie Miller, Ryan Peter Murphy, Leslie Odom Jr., Keke Palmer, Anthony Ramos, RIIZE and Smash Mouth will also perform.

Jack McBrayer, Janet McTeer, John Stamos, Melissa Joan Hart, Megan Hilty, Holly Robinson Peete and Rodney Peete are also scheduled to appear.

articles.title: DC's Original Superboy Series Began With This Rare Comic, and One of Its Finest Copies Is Up for Auction
articles.summary: In the late forties, super-heroes were a dying breed. articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google In the late forties, super-heroes were a dying breed. The "Golden Age" of super-hero comics was short-lived, and by the end of the same decade that spawned them, characters like the Flash , Green Lantern , and Captain America were in danger of cancellation. One of the sole exceptions was Superman , who, propelled by an incredibly popular radio series (soon to be adapted to television), was still appearing in three regular comic book titles: Action Comics, Superman , and World's Finest . Sales were so strong that DC elected to launch a fourth in 1949, Superboy , centered on the adventures of the Man of Steel when he was a teenager in Smallville. Owing to its vintage, and the younger audience the comic was geared toward, few copies of its inaugural issue survive into the modern era, with the CGC (Certified Guarantee Company)'s population report listing just two hundred and ninety graded copies in existence. Of these, only two dozen exist in the same or better condition than this CGC-graded 8.0 , up for auction later in the week through Heritage.

The Superboy comic wasn't the first time readers met an adolescent Superman, but it did mark a transition into Superboy stories as a regular feature of DC Comics. The adventures of Superboy were a surprisingly key part of DC's pre- Crisis On Infinite Earths continuity, virtually ubiquitous in the 1950s and 1960s. These were featured not only in Superboy , but Action Comics and Adventure Comics . Some of the most iconic characters, teams, and concepts in the DC Universe would debut in Superboy stories, which introduced readers to the Phantom Zone, the Legion of Super-Heroes, and Krypto the Super-Dog. Post- Crisis, in typically convoluted comic book fashion, the name would come to represent not just Clark Kent, but his clone and his son. Superboy #1 marks the true beginning of that history, and the chance to add it to their collection has comic fans bidding $8.9k and counting.

At its best, Superboy was nothing short of camp. DC assumed a younger readership for the title, and wrote its stories to suit: logic was loose, action was fast-paced, and the plots uncomplex. Fifties Superboy stories usually found him performing impossible feats of derring-do, becoming one of the " Hep-Cats of Smallville ," or " the One-Man Baseball Team ." These were written by middle-aged men with no concept of what was hip, trying to appeal to kids based on what they read in the newspaper or saw on TV. The results are gloriously silly, and leave you constantly asking whether or not they were in on the joke. However, these comics came with a surprisingly poignant side: Superboy was a distinct character from Superman, less sure of himself and reliant on the love and support of Ma and Pa Kent — who had since passed away by the time we meet the full-grown Man of Steel in Action Comics #1. Similarly, the beloved Krypto the Super-Dog featured predominantly in Superboy's adventures, as did Clark Kent's first love, Lana Lang. Perhaps even unintentionally, Superboy was a window into a happier time in Superman's life, and a reminder how lonely the inhabitant of the "Fortress of Solitude" really was.

By the end of the fifties, Krypto's appearances in the title became more regular, underlining an increased focus on science fiction plots and costumed supporting characters for DC's Superboy titles. 1958 saw Superboy introduce its first significant DC character, Bizarro, in issue #68. Though he evolved into a comic character in subsequent appearances, Bizarro is a tragic Frankenstein-like figure in Superboy #68, created in a lab accident designed to duplicate Superboy. Bizarro Superboy destroys himself at the issue's close, returning as Bizarro Superman in Action Comics #254 the following year. It was in Action Comics that Bizarro and Bizarro-World would be developed into fixtures of the Superman titles, even appearing as a back-up feature to Superboy in Adventure Comics . It was also in this era that the Phantom Zone became a regular plot device, usually for the introduction of an escaped Phantom Zone Criminal to challenge the Boy of Steel. General Zod is the best known of these, debuting alongside the Phantom Zone itself in Adventure Comics #283.

Superboy was also a home for Legion of Super-Heroes stories, following the team's debut in Adventure Comics #247. The time-travelling heroes were a handy solution to several problems posed by the flashback nature of Superboy stories. They allowed writers to circumvent the problem of many of DC's other heroes not taking on their super-hero identity until adulthood, as well as the question of their absence during Superman's adult years. Especially handy in this respect is the Legion's hilariously arbitrary rule that members must be under eighteen years of age, another example of the sometimes baffling internal logic that these stories functioned under. Legionnaires Mon-El and Ultra-Boy debuted in Superboy, which transitioned into Superboy Starring the Legion of Super-Heroes (later Superboy and the Legion of Super-Heroes ) with issue #197 in 1973.

Sales for Superboy waned as the sixties wore on, a symptom of DC's increasingly close competition with Marvel Comics. The title lacked creative direction, and its episodic storytelling began to feel outmoded by the serialized, continuity heavy work of writers like Stan Lee and Roy Thomas. Its tone also became a problem, as Marvel and DC alike were able to court an older readership demographic with many of their titles. Comics had become cool, and Superboy was everything about them that wasn't. Even superstar artist Neal Adams could do little to bolster the title's flagging popularity in the late sixties, and by 1973, DC made the decision to transition Superboy into a Legion of Super-Heroes comic. He remained primary character in the comic until #259, when the Superboy was dropped from the title and it became Legion of Super-Heroes, with Superboy headlining the New Adventures of Superboy beginning that month. Curiously, Legion of Super-Heroes retained the numbering from the original Superboy series, rather than New Adventures of Superboy .

The New Adventures of Superboy ran a respectable fifty-four issues, wrapping up in 1984. It marked the last time a comic would feature "the Adventures of Superman When He Was a Boy," as 1986's universe-wide reset Crisis on Infinite Earths would render Superboy's history and existence non-canon. A new Superboy title debuted in 1990, focused on Clark Kent's college years and originally intended as a tie-in for the short-lived Superboy television series . A new Superboy was introduced in 1993 as part of the "Reign of the Supermen" storyline, serving as one of several replacements to Superman in the wake of the "Death of Superman" storyline. The new Superboy was Connor Kent, a clone of Superman grown in a lab by the Cadmus corporation. Connor Kent is likely the "Superboy" most modern readers know best, appearing as the DC Universe's primary Superboy up until the Rebirth reboot, as well as starring in the fan favorite Young Justice cartoon .

The New 52 retained a reimagined Connor Kent as Superboy, using largely the same Superman clone backstory. For Rebirth , a third Superboy replaced Connor Kent: Jonathan Kent, the son of Clark Kent and Lois Lane. Like the original Silver Age Clark Kent Superboy, Jonathan Kent has enabled creators and readers to explore a different side of the Superman character. Through Jonathan, we see what Clark Kent is like as a father, providing real change and evolution in a medium noted for its frequent refusal to let characters grow . Somehow, Superboy has become one of the most malleable concepts in the DC Universe, much more complex than the simple pitch of "Superman but when he was younger." Maybe it's because of the difference in age and maturity, which enables readers to see a more flawed character that better reflects us. Pre- Crisis , Superman is portrayed as always having all the answers, whereas Superboy didn't. Post- Rebirth , Superboy lets us see the one place the adult Superman doesn't have all the answers: parenthood. The character is a reminder that what makes super-heroes human is what makes them heroic. That's embodied by the cover to Superboy #1, where Superman literally opens up to a group of children, inviting them to learn more about his life, and maybe through it, learn to be a little more like him.

What's your favorite incarnation of Superboy? Leave a comment below and join the conversation now in the ComicBook Forum !

articles.title: Roseanne Writer Said She Made Things ‘Hard’ On Set. Why He Still Felt Bad For Her
articles.summary: The Connors weren't the only ones having a rough time.
articles.content:
There's plenty to keep up with on the 2026 TV schedule , and I can't say revisiting Roseanne Barr was high on my list. But whenever her name comes up, it's hard to forget just how enormous Roseanne was when it debuted. The sitcom gave working-class families a voice network TV didn't always bother with, and Barr was a big reason it worked. Unfortunately, the stories about what went on behind the scenes haven't always been nearly as warm. Now one of the original show's head writers is looking back on those difficult early days, and his recollection of Barr might surprise you.

I find that an interesting way to remember somebody you worked with, especially decades later. Jacobson hasn't forgotten the headaches, but he watched a stand-up comic become the face of one of TV's biggest shows almost overnight. Barr made her breakthrough on The Tonight Show in 1985. By 1988, she was headlining an ABC sitcom built around her distinctive comic voice.

I like that he ends with the work, because there's a reason people are still talking about Roseanne almost 40 years later. The series could be incredibly funny, but it also let the Conners worry about money and have family arguments that weren't neatly resolved before the credits. It felt familiar in a way many more polished sitcom families didn't.

Jacobson also recalled that Barr learned to act quickly, with considerable help from Goodman and Metcalf. That's a pretty fantastic pair of co-workers to have when you're figuring out sitcom acting on the fly. Their chemistry helped make the Conners believable. Interestingly, Goodman has also spoken about defending his former co-star , so Jacobson isn't the only person who worked with Barr and still has some sympathy for her.

articles.title: 'I Play Rocky' Stars Unite With Original 'Rocky' Producer for Film's 50th Anniversary Celebration
articles.summary: Irwin Winkler, who was behind Sylvester Stallone's 1976 hit, joined Anthony Ippolito, AnnaSophia Robb and director Peter Farrelly at the Academy Museum event.
articles.content:
Rocky minds old and new came together on Tuesday night for a 50th anniversary celebration of Sylvester Stallone 's breakout 1976 hit.

The iconic boxing movie is back in the culture not only for its milestone anniversary but also because of I Play Rocky , which chronicles Stallone's journey of bringing his project to the big screen. At the event — held at the Academy Museum — I Play Rocky stars Anthony Ippolito , AnnaSophia Robb, P.J. Byrne and Kiki Seto, director Peter Farrelly and writer Peter Gamble were all in attendance, alongside Rocky producer Irwin Winkler . (They also stopped by a THR photo studio inside of Fanny's restaurant, with images below.) blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Lifestyle THR Celebrates Hollywood's New Wave of Stars at Next Gen Dinner Movies The Sound of Rocky: How an Anthem Was Born

Winkler took the stage for a Q&A before the special screening of Rocky , recalling how Stallone came in for a meeting and mentioned the story he had in mind. "He said he would write the story very quickly, with the understanding that if we liked the script, we had to star him in the film," Winkler remembered of the star's comments to him and fellow producer Robert Chartoff. "And the rest you'll see on I Play Rocky . It really told the story very, very well, probably better than I could."

The producer added that "we made this little movie for a million dollars, we didn't expect anything out of it" but credits its uplifting message — following the Vietnam War and Watergate where "people were really kind of down and depressed" — for its success. "This movie came along and said, 'America is also a place if you believe in yourself, you have the opportunity to succeed.' And I think, in a strange way, I think we're back to some of the same feelings," Winkler said. "I think what I Play Rocky shows you is the story about a man who believes in himself, that America can give you that opportunity to succeed. I don't want to sound political but I can't help it." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Winkler also touched on the spinoff Creed films, saying "We thought we had put the franchise to bed with Rocky Balboa " but upon meeting Ryan Coogler, "he had the same passion that Stallone had shown 40 years before" and "I said to myself, 'If we're going to ever make another Rocky , I want to make it with this young Ryan Coogler.'"

Midway through the conversation, Winkler was joined by Farrelly and Ippolito; the filmmaker recalled watching Rocky as a freshman in college and "I remember walking out of the theater, being like, 'Woo, woo!' And I didn't know what I was wooing about, but I was pumped up — to do what? I have no idea. But I was inspired, and I remember going back to school and getting my buddies and being like, 'OK, you've got to see this movie.' The closest I could compare it to is like having a sports team. It was like you fell in love with a sports team, and you were rooting for him, and Rocky was our team."

Farrelly also called I Play Rocky "the best script I ever read," noting, "the thing that grabbed me the most was that I realized this movie mirrors Rocky . It's very similar. It was like [Stallone] was telling his own story." Winkler said he questioned how Gamble knew so many of the inside details he put in the script and was surprised to find so much of the information available online. He also joked, "watching P.J. Byrne play me, I was a bit surprised because I thought Brad Pitt would really be me. But I'll take P.J. anytime." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Ippolito closed out the chat by musing that Rocky 's success is because "the underdog story is a very universal one. I think everybody has a Rocky inside of them. I think we all have our own personal relationship to this story and to this character," adding, "it's an incredible, incredible film. You guys got great taste being here tonight."

articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Pokemon fans have today been given their first look at Flowing Fists , which is the first new expansion for the Pokemon Trading Card Game launching in 2027. Earlier this month, Pokemon TCG released Delta Reign , which was the sixth expansion as part of the ongoing Mega Evolution set. And while many Pokemon TCG fans are still trying to collect all of the biggest cards that are part of Delta Reign , we now have a better idea of what's coming down the line.

Shown off on social media, Pokemon TCG revealed a handful of the first cards that will be part of Flowing Fists . This time around, Mega Lucario Z will be the mascot for the expansion, which makes sense given its name. Mega Lucario Z will be joined by Mega Absol Z, Mega Glimmora, and Mega Garchomp as some of the most notable Pokemon to receive new EX cards. In total, Flowing Fists will have over 110 cards, with 9 EX cards, 11 IR cards, 18 ultra rare cards, and 6 SIR cards.

Step into new powers and unlock the potential of Mega Lucario Z ex and other cool Pokémon in Pokémon TCG: Mega Evolution—Flowing Fists! 👊 Available starting February 6! Subsequent Pokémon TCG expansions will continue to release on Saturdays. pic.twitter.com/OnIVEF6C9a

As for its release, Flowing Fists will also be making a change from how Pokemon TCG has operated in the past. This expansion will be launching early next year on February 6, 2027. While this might not seem like anything crazy, Flowing Fists will actually be releasing on a Saturday. Historically, new Pokemon TCG expansions and sets have released on Fridays, which means that Flowing Fists is making a slight deviation from the norm. Moving forward, these Saturday releases will become standard for future Pokemon TCG sets as well.

Per usual, Flowing Fists will also be sold in a number of different ways. Outside of standard booster packs, this new Pokemon TCG expansion will also launch with an Elite Trainer Box, which will notably come with a Riolu promo card, a collector's box, and unique card sleeves. Booster boxes, booster bundles, and a Build & Battle bundle will also be released, allowing fans to get their hands on numerous packs at once.

Currently, pre-orders for Pokemon TCG's Flowing Fists expansion haven't gone live, but that should change as we approach its February launch. Pre-release events for the expansion are expected to transpire between January 23rd and January 31st. As such, if you want to be amongst the first to get your hands on these new cards, you'll want to attend one of these events for yourself.

How do you feel about Flowing Fists based on what we've seen so far? And which card in this set are you planning to chase above the rest? Be sure to let me know for yourself down in the comments section.

articles.content:
Keltie Knight is a three-time Emmy–winning television personality, New York Times bestselling author, and People’s Choice Award–nominated podcast host ("LadyGang"). She currently hosts "E! Live From the Red Carpet" and is widely known for her work on "Entertainment Tonight," "The Insider," and CBS’s "Superfan," which she also created and executive produced.

In this excerpt from her latest book, "The F*ck Them Theory: Self-Help For People Who are Done Being the Bigger Person" (available Nov. 24 from Blackstone Publishing), Knight recounts the trials she faced after creating "Superfan" — including a lawsuit from rival producers — and what she learned from surviving all the drama. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Jennifer Lopez on the ‘JLo Show’ Concert Film, Her ‘Happy Era’ and Moving on From Divorce: 'What I Thought Love Was Really Isn’t Love’ Robert Pattinson Is Officially James Bond: Meet the New 007 Actor

I use all that rage to fuel my next big idea, but what happens when the haters are right? I swear, every time something incredible happens to me, the universe immediately follows it with a slap across the face. I don't even like to celebrate my wins anymore; I just start bracing for the chaos that's about to roll in. It's like the universe can't stand to see me strut for more than twenty-four hours before serving me a fresh slice of humble pie.

That's exactly what happened when I sold my first primetime TV series, "Superfan."

I'd been in the television business long enough to know that no one was ever going to hand me a dream gig. I watched as my friends all got auditions to host new game shows, competition series, and did on-screen tests for shows like "The View" and "Today." There was always something new and exciting going on in the hosting world, but I rarely got called in, and in the end Mario Lopez usually ended up booking it. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

As frustrating as it was, if I wanted to be at the top of someone's list, I was going to have to build my own damn list. So I did. I created, pitched, and sold my own primetime network show. (Author's note: This would be a great thing to put on my epitaph if you want me to truly rest in peace.)

This is something that statistically almost never happens for women. A 2022 study by Women in Film found that in 2018, women-owned production companies received 18.6 percent of studio-subsidized film deals and 35.7 percent of studio-subsidized television deals. A 2024 report noted that women accounted for just 23 percent of creators employed across broadcast and streaming television programs. The numbers are beyond dismal. And on this project I even had a female business partner. Picture us: two women with solid résumés, zero hit shows, no famous last names, and definitely no family money.

The idea had lived in my brain for years. A shiny floor musical competition show where superfans of the biggest artists all competed to be named the number one fan, winning an insane prize package like the chance to sing on stage with the artist. I even paid $11 to register it with the Writers Guild back in 2016. (That's Hollywood's version of a patent. It's cheap, hopeful, and usually useless.) I'd filed that paper away, secretly proud but mostly convinced it would never matter. But this time, it did. The thing I dreamed up actually sold.

When Variety printed the announcement, my face next to "CBS Orders Musical Competition Series," I could barely breathe. It was one of the proudest moments of my entire career. I'd done it. After years of hosting other people's dreams, I had finally built my own.

Business Affairs. Cold tone. Legalese. A group of men (of course it was men) believed the network had stolen their pitch and handed it to us instead. They were threatening to sue.

I laughed when I first heard the accusation. Really? If the network was going to steal a format, don't you think they'd give it to someone who created "Survivor" or "The Amazing Race"? Not to the girl from the LadyGang podcast? But logic doesn't matter in Hollywood. What matters is drama.

And just like that, my dream was now a liability.

Every email came with an asterisk. Every call ended in "we'll see." I woke up every morning thinking, My show is getting made, followed by I'm getting sued. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

I knew the idea was mine. I had the timestamped deck, the registration, and the receipts. But if you've ever been threatened with a lawsuit, you know that facts don't keep you calm, especially when your husband once managed Robin Thicke and Pharrell through the "Blurred Lines" musical lawsuit. A case where the jury sided with vibes and personality over facts. (None of the notes were the same, guys! Not a single one!) Truth and justice don't always RSVP to the same meeting.

Still, I kept going. What else was I supposed to do?

For two years we worked. We waited. We developed. We prayed. We pushed through, hoping it would all work out.

While we waited for the pending lawsuit to get cleared up and an air date for the show, we started pitching "Superfan" internationally. We flew to MIPCOM in France, the global TV marketplace. I thought: This is it. The rebirth.

Except my producing partner got sick the second we landed. I walked into the pitch rooms alone. Foreign buyers. Language barriers. Me smiling, sweating, hustling like I was twenty-five again. And it worked. France wanted it. Other countries did too. We were finally building momentum, and we were all set to become the next global sensation!

When we got back from France, the network started discussing shutting it all down. They might just never air "Superfan" at all. They said the potential lawsuit meant we couldn't sell internationally. The worldwide deals vanished. The enthusiasm faded. We weren't the fresh new hit anymore. We were the problematic project.

"Superfan" did finally air, but it was eighteen months late. That's a lifetime in television. By the time it dropped, most people had forgotten we'd even filmed it. All our celebrities were singing year-old hits. Some had even dropped entirely new albums. The network didn't really promote it. It was dropped like a half-empty water bottle on a hot day, technically delivered, but with no care.

To everyone else, this was the end. A quiet burial for a show no one believed in. But I wasn't about to let that happen. I'd worked too hard. I had poured years of my life into this project, and even if the powers that be had already moved on, I hadn't.

So I did what I always do: I made something out of nothing. I manufactured my own miracle. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

I begged my husband, who had connections from working with a billboard company at the time, to help me throw a splashy premiere in Times Square. I invited everyone: network heads, influencers, friends. I convinced Getty Images to shoot it like it was the Grammys. I even paid for LL Cool J's private jet out of my own pocket (!!) because he was our debut episode's star, and I knew we needed star power if we were going to make anyone pay attention to our dead-on-arrival series. I was praying that my evil genius plan would turn "Superfan" into the next "Seinfeld."

Did you know "Seinfeld," one of the most successful sitcoms in TV history, was originally considered a total flop by test audiences and network focus groups? When NBC first piloted the show, the focus group results were brutal. Viewers described it as "too New York," "too Jewish," and "too self-indulgent." One network report labeled it "weak" and said it would "not be a success." NBC executives joked that it was "a show about nothing, and maybe should stay that way." The original pilot scored so low with test audiences that NBC nearly didn't order any episodes at all. The only reason "Seinfeld" survived was because a few network champions believed in Jerry Seinfeld and Larry David's unique voice and fought for a limited four-episode order.

Those four episodes led to nine seasons, ten Emmy Awards, and billions in syndication revenue. The data said no. The suits said no. They were all wrong.

But the focus groups weren't wrong about "Superfan." The reviews were brutal. Headlines called us a "superflop." Ouch. We underperformed and never recovered.

And then, while I was having dinner in the backyard with my husband and father-in-law, a stranger walked up and handed me a manila envelope. I'd been served. Those men sued us anyway.

Six more months. Stress. Embarrassment. Anxiety. All over a show the world didn't even want.

But I know the universe wasn't punishing me. It was preparing me.

When people ask, "How do you stay so motivated?"

Every rejection is fuel. Every derailment? A redirection. I learned so much from my flop; it was a masterclass.

Rejection isn't a dead end. It's a test. It's the universe making sure you're strong enough for what's next. The only real rejection that matters is the one where you reject yourself. Don't do that. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid4' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

If winning were easy, everyone would be doing it. If staying in the game didn't require total ego death, none of us would evolve. If rejection stings? It means you cared enough to try.

Rejection isn't failure. Every no proves you're brave enough to show up. Every almost-great flop says: You took a risk.

Fuck rejection. Keep going. Keep showing up. Keep becoming.
